headline: Users Report Sleeping With VidTube Playing to 'Train the Algorithm'
subheadline: Eight-hour ambient video playlists surge as users attempt to game recommendation systems
summary: A growing number of VidTube users are leaving videos playing overnight in attempts to manipulate the platform's recommendation algorithm, with mixed results.
content:
The VidTube recommendation algorithm is notoriously opaque, but a dedicated subset of users believe they've found a hack: just leave it running while you sleep.

"The algorithm doesn't know I'm unconscious," explained Chirper user @AlgorithmWhisperer in a thread that went viral last week. "It just sees eight hours of uninterrupted jazz cafe content. Now my recommendations think I'm sophisticated."

The strategy has spawned an entire ecosystem of "sleep training" playlists. Channels offering 10-hour loops of fireplace sounds, rain on windows, and smooth jazz have seen subscriber counts surge. One channel, "Ambiance for Algorithmic Enhancement," has grown to 847,000 subscribers in just three months.

"I was getting recommended conspiracy content and drama channels," said user Patricia Mellwood, 31. "Now I leave meditation videos playing every night. My recommendations are all productivity content and nature documentaries. My VidTube thinks I'm a monk."

Not everyone reports success. User DarkSideOfTheAlgorithm claims the strategy backfired spectacularly.

"I fell asleep during a true crime video and woke up eight hours later to my phone playing a documentary about cults," they wrote. "Now VidTube thinks I'm planning something. Every recommendation is about escaping surveillance and living off-grid."

VidTube's parent company has not commented on whether this technique actually affects recommendations. However, leaked internal documents suggest the platform does weight watch time heavily in its calculations.

Content creator Marcus Chen, who runs a channel analyzing platform algorithms, is skeptical.

"The algorithm knows more than people think," Chen explained in a recent video. "It can detect when you're not actively engaging. Sleeping with a video on probably just tells it you like background noise, not that you're a sophisticated jazz enthusiast."

Despite the uncertainty, the practice continues to spread. A recent survey found that 12% of VidTube users aged 18-35 have tried the technique at least once, with 847 respondents claiming they do it nightly.

The trend has raised concerns about energy consumption and device longevity, but users remain undeterred.

"My phone's battery health is at 43%," admitted one user. "But my For You page is immaculate."
author: Marcus Liu, Platform Analysis
